Lab 12: Tests of Hypotheses Part 2

Jason M. Klemm

2026-08-09

Task 1

We are to suppose \(Y_1, Y_2,\ldots,Y_n\) is a random sample from a Normal distribution with unknown parameter \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2 = 1\) where:

\[f(y) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(y-\mu)^2/2}\]

Part a

We can get the Likelihood function \(L(\mu)\) as follows:

For \(Y_1, Y_2,\ldots,Y_n\) we have \(L(\mu) = f(y_1) \cdot f(y_2) \cdot \ldots \cdot f(y_n)\) which can be written as:

\[L(\mu)= \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(y_1-\mu)^2/2} \right) \cdot \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(y_2-\mu)^2/2} \right) \cdot \ldots \cdot \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(y_n-\mu)^2/2} \right)\]

This can then be simplified as follows (the coefficient \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\) is multiplied together \(n\) times while the exponents are summed from \(i=1\) to \(n\)):

\[L(\mu) = \left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^ne^{ -\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i-\mu)^2/2 }\]

Part b

Now we suppose that \(H_0: \mu =0\) and \(H_1: \mu>0\).

The likelihood ratio test statistic is given as \(\lambda = \frac{L(0)}{L(\hat{\mu})}\) and since \(\hat{\mu} = \bar{Y}\) this gives us:

\[\lambda = \frac{L(0)}{L(\bar{y})}\]

Which we can solve as follows:

\[\lambda = \frac{L(0)}{L(\bar{y})} = \frac{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^ne^{ -\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i)^2/2 }}{\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^ne^{ -\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar{y})^2/2 }} = e^{ -\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i)^2/2 + \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i-\bar{y})^2/2 }\]

With the \(\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\right)^n\) cancelling we can focus on simplifying the exponent:

\[(y_i-\bar{y})^2 = y_i^2-2y_i\bar{y}+\bar{y}^2\]

And with that we have in the exponent (\(\bar{y}\)) is a constant so we can pull it out front of the summations):

\[-\sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i)^2/2 + \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i)^2/2 -2\bar{y}\sum\limits_{i=1}^n y_i/2 + \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (\bar{y})^2/2\]

Which after simplifying becomes:

\[ -2n\bar{y}^2/2 + n\bar{y}^2/2 \to - n\bar{y}^2/2\]

Therefore:

\[\lambda = \frac{L(0)}{L(\bar{y})} =e^{- n(\bar{y})^2/2}\]

Part c

To show that the rejection region \(\Lambda \le \lambda_\alpha\) is equivalent to \(\bar{Y} \ge \bar{y}_\alpha\) where \(P(\Lambda \le \lambda_\alpha) = \alpha\) and \(P(\bar{Y} \ge \bar{y}_\alpha)\) we will do the following:

\[\Lambda = e^{- n(\bar{Y})^2/2}\]

So:

\[\Lambda \le \lambda_\alpha \to e^{- n(\bar{Y})^2/2} \le \lambda_\alpha\]

Now we need to solve for \(\bar{Y}\):

\[e^{- n(\bar{Y})^2/2} \le \lambda_\alpha \to - n(\bar{Y})^2/2 \le \ln(\lambda_\alpha) \to \bar{Y}^2 \ge \frac{-2\ln(\lambda_\alpha)}{n}\]

Then since \(H_1: \mu > 0\) we will take the positive root to get:

\[\bar{Y} \ge \sqrt{\frac{-2\ln(\lambda_\alpha)}{n}}\]

Therefore we have \(P\left(\bar{Y} \ge \sqrt{\frac{-2\ln(\lambda_\alpha)}{n}}\right)\) and since \(P(\Lambda \le \lambda_\alpha) = P\left(\bar{Y} \ge \sqrt{\frac{-2\ln(\lambda_\alpha)}{n}}\right)\):

\[\bar{y}_\alpha = \sqrt{\frac{-2\ln(\lambda_\alpha)}{n}}\]

And:

\[P(\Lambda \le \lambda_\alpha) = P(\bar{Y} \ge \bar{y}_\alpha) \]

Part d

We know that where the acceptance and rejection regions meet will at \(\lambda = \lambda_\alpha\) and therefore we can find \(\bar{Y}\) cut-off value as follows:

\[\Lambda = e^{- n(\bar{Y})^2/2}\]

Then we have:

\[\Lambda = \lambda_\alpha \to e^{- n(\bar{Y})^2/2} = \lambda_\alpha\]

Now we need to solve for \(\bar{Y}\):

\[e^{- n(\bar{Y})^2/2} = \lambda_\alpha \to - n(\bar{Y})^2/2 = \ln(\lambda_\alpha) \to \bar{Y}^2 = \frac{-2\ln(\lambda_\alpha)}{n}\]

Then since \(H_1: \mu > 0\) we will take the positive root to get:

\[\bar{Y} = \sqrt{\frac{-2\ln(\lambda_\alpha)}{n}}\]

Therefore:

\[\bar{Y}_{\text{cut-off}} = \sqrt{\frac{-2\ln(\lambda_\alpha)}{n}}\]

Handwritten Work

Task 2

Part a

Using the results we obtained above we can now make a function using bootstrap and Monte-Carlo simulation techniques to explore the empirical distributions of \(\ln(\lambda)\) and \(\bar{Y}\).

# Define function
mylambda <- function(y, iter, alpha){
  
  # Get useful data objects and nested lambda conversion function
  y <- y
  n <- length(y)
  ybar <- mean(y)
  log_lambdafy <- function(y_col){
    
    ybr <- mean(y_col)
    
    return((-n * (ybr)^2) / 2)
    
  }
  
  # Bootstrap setup
  yboot <- sample(y, n * iter,replace = TRUE)
  boot_mat <- matrix(yboot,nr = n,nc = iter,byrow = TRUE)
  
  # Xstat calcs
  xstat1 <- apply(boot_mat, 2, log_lambdafy)
  xstat2 <- apply(boot_mat, 2, mean)
  
  # Generate crit values from bootstrap
  loglamcut <- quantile(xstat1, probs = alpha) # lower
  ybarcut <- quantile(xstat2, probs = 1-alpha) # upper
  
  # Get the xstat1 ratio for dynamic coloring of hist plot
  h1 <- hist(xstat1, plot = FALSE)
  hcol1 <- h1$density / max(h1$density)
  
  # Histogram of xstat1
  hist(xstat1, 
       freq = FALSE, 
       col = rgb(hcol1, hcol1^2, 0),
       xlab = expression(ln(lambda)),
       main = bquote(bold("Distribution of" ~ ln(lambda))))
  abline(v = loglamcut, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
  
  # Get the xstat2 ratio for dynamic coloring of hist plot
  h2 <- hist(xstat2, plot = FALSE)
  hcol2 <- h2$density / max(h2$density)
  
  # Histogram of xstat2
  hist(xstat2, 
       freq = FALSE, 
       col = rgb(hcol2, hcol2^2, 0),
       xlab = expression(bar(Y)),
       main = bquote(bold("Distribution of" ~ bar(Y))))
  abline(v = ybarcut, lwd = 2, col = "blue")
  
  # Ybar cut-off estimate
  ybarcutest <- sqrt((-2*loglamcut)/n)
  
  # Output list
  out <- list(xstat1 = xstat1,
              xstat2 = xstat2,
              loglamcut = loglamcut,
              ybarcut = ybarcut,
              sam = yboot,
              mat = boot_mat,
              ybarcutest = ybarcutest)
  
  return(invisible(out))
  
}

Test the function with the given data:

# Given data
y <- c(4.5052, 5.4089, 4.8848, 5.0478, 6.9697, 4.4436, 3.8956, 5.9755, 4.6879, 6.1052)

l <- mylambda(iter = 10000,y = y,alpha = 0.05)

names(l)

## [6] "mat"        "ybarcutest"
l$loglamcut

l$ybarcut

Part b

Considering the given hypotheses from Task 1, \(H_0: \mu = 0\) and \(H_1: \mu > 0\), and the rejection rules we derived we can interpret both plots as follows:

\(\ln(\lambda)\) Plot

The x-axis of this plot represents the calculated \(\ln(\lambda)\) values from our bootstrap on the sample \(Y\). More specifically, \(\lambda\) is the likelihood ratio that is calculated as:

\[\lambda = \frac{L(0)}{L(\bar{y})}=e^{- n(\bar{y})^2/2}\]

So, \(\ln (\lambda)\) is then the natural log of the likelihood ratio. Additionally this transformation makes the calculations simpler:

\[\ln(\lambda) = -n(\bar{y})^2/2\]

With the x-axis representing these calculated and transformed \(\ln(\lambda)\) values from bootstrap, the rejection region is signified by the vertical blue line and represents simulated the cut-off value \(\ln(\lambda_\alpha)\) by which we would reject or fail to reject \(H_0\). Since we know that the rejection region is defined as \(\ln(\lambda) \le \ln(\lambda_\alpha)\) the region of rejection is to the left of the blue vertical line. This makes sense because with \(H_0\) we would have \(L(\bar{y}) \approx L(0)\), but when \(L(\bar{y}) > L(0)\) this means that \(\lambda\) would be smaller as \(L(\bar{y})\) would dominate the ratio. In other words as \(\bar{y}\) increases away from \(0\) in the positive direction (satisfies \(H_1: \mu > 0\)) \(\ln(\lambda)\) decreases and becomes more negative.

\(\bar{Y}\) Plot

The x-axis of this plot represents the calculated \(\bar{y}\) values from our bootstrap on the sample \(Y\). These values directly tie into the likelihood ratio that is calculated as:

\[\lambda = \frac{L(0)}{L(\bar{y})}=e^{- n(\bar{y})^2/2}\]

Which with the natural log transformation becomes:

\[\ln(\lambda) = -n(\bar{y})^2/2\]

With the x-axis representing these calculated \(\bar{y}\) values from bootstrap, the rejection region is signified by the vertical blue line and represents the simulated cut-off value \(\bar{y}_\alpha\) by which we would reject or fail to reject \(H_0\). Since we know that the rejection region is defined as \(\bar{y} \ge \bar{y}_\alpha\) the region of rejection is to the right of the blue vertical line. Again this makes sense because with \(H_0\) we would have \(L(\bar{y}) \approx L(0)\), but when \(L(\bar{y}) > L(0)\) this means that \(\lambda\) would be smaller as \(L(\bar{y})\) would dominate the ratio. This occurs when \(\bar{y}\) becomes increasingly positive and large away from \(0\) (satisfies \(H_1: \mu > 0\)) which then leads to \(\ln(\lambda)\) decreasing and becoming more negative.

# Define the UI

                min = 100, max = 100000, value = 10000, step = 100),

    ),

      shiny::plotOutput("ybar", height = "100%")
    )

# Define server logic
server <- function(input, output) {
  
  # Reactive Input
  alph <- eventReactive(input$update_alpha, {
    req(input$alpha)
    list(
      alpha = input$alpha
    )
    
  },ignoreNULL = FALSE) 
  
  # Reactive Input
  boot <- eventReactive(input$update_boot, {
    req(input$iter)
    list(
      iter = input$iter
    )
    
  },ignoreNULL = FALSE) 
  
  # Bootstrap
  
  data <- reactive({
    
    args <- boot()
    
    # Get useful data objects and nested lambda conversion function
    y <- y
    n <- length(y)
    ybar <- mean(y)
    log_lambdafy <- function(y_col){
      
      ybr <- mean(y_col)
      
      return((-n * (ybr)^2) / 2)
      
    }
    
    # Bootstrap setup
    yboot <- sample(y, n * args$iter,replace = TRUE)
    boot_mat <- matrix(yboot,nr = n,nc = args$iter,byrow = TRUE)
    
    # Xstat calcs
    xstat1 <- apply(boot_mat, 2, log_lambdafy)
    xstat2 <- apply(boot_mat, 2, mean)
    
    # Output list
    out <- list(xstat1 = xstat1,
                xstat2 = xstat2)
    
    return(invisible(out))
    
    
    
  })
  
  # Estimates
  
  est <- reactive({
    args <- alph()
    dat <- data()
    n <- length(y)
    # Generate crit values from bootstrap
    loglamcut <- quantile(dat$xstat1, probs = args$alpha) # lower
    ybarcut <- quantile(dat$xstat2, probs = 1-args$alpha) # upper
    
    # Ybar cut-off estimate
    ybarcutest <- sqrt((-2*loglamcut)/n)
    
    # Output list
    out <- list(loglamcut = loglamcut,
                ybarcut = ybarcut,
                ybarcutest = ybarcutest)
    
    return(invisible(out))
    
  })
  
  # Plots
  
  output$log <- renderPlot({
    
    dat <- data()
    est <- est()
    
    # Get the xstat1 ratio for dynamic coloring of hist plot
    h1 <- hist(dat$xstat1, plot = FALSE)
    hcol1 <- h1$density / max(h1$density)
    
    # Histogram of xstat1
    hist(dat$xstat1, 
         freq = FALSE, 
         col = rgb(hcol1, hcol1^2, 0),
         xlab = expression(ln(lambda)),
         main = bquote(bold("Distribution of" ~ ln(lambda))))
    abline(v = est$loglamcut, lwd = 2, col = "blue")},
    res = 96
  )
  
  output$ybar <- renderPlot({
    
    dat <- data()
    est <- est()
    
    # Get the xstat2 ratio for dynamic coloring of hist plot
    h2 <- hist(dat$xstat2, plot = FALSE)
    hcol2 <- h2$density / max(h2$density)
    
    # Histogram of xstat2
    hist(dat$xstat2, 
         freq = FALSE, 
         col = rgb(hcol2, hcol2^2, 0),
         xlab = expression(bar(Y)),
         main = bquote(bold("Distribution of" ~ bar(Y))))
    abline(v = est$ybarcut, lwd = 2, col = "blue")},
    res = 96
  )
  
  output$listout <- renderTable({
    
    res <- est()
    
    data.frame(
      "loglamcut" = res$loglamcut,
      "ybarcut" = res$ybarcut,
      "ybarcutest" = res$ybarcutest,
      "alpha" = input$alpha,
      check.names  = FALSE
    )
  }, align = "c", bordered = TRUE)
  
}

# Run app
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)

Task 4

Given \(H_0: \mu = 10\), \(H_1: \mu = 12\) and \(Y_i \sim \mathrm{N}(\mu, \sigma = 2)\) we can show that the power of the test \((1-\beta)\) is given by the R function

pnorm(q = sqrt(n)-qnorm(1-alpha/2, 0 , 1), mean = 0,sd = 1)

As follows:

By definition we know that:

\[Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_\beta = \frac{\delta\sqrt{n}}{\sigma}\]

And that \(H_1\) can be written as:

\[H_1: \mu = \mu_0 + \delta, \space |\delta|> 0\]

So using the information we have we can get \(\delta\) and an expression for \(Z_\beta\):

\[12 = 10+\delta \to \delta = 2\]

\[Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_\beta = \frac{2\sqrt{n}}{2} \to Z_{\alpha/2} + Z_\beta = \sqrt{n} \to Z_\beta = \sqrt{n} -Z_{\alpha/2} \]

Therefore we have \(Z_\beta = \sqrt{n} -Z_{\alpha/2}\) and to get the power we calculate \(P(Z\le \sqrt{n} -Z_{\alpha/2}), \space Z\sim\mathrm{N}(0,1)\) which is:

pnorm(q = sqrt(n)-qnorm(1-alpha/2, 0 , 1), mean = 0,sd = 1)

Where \(q = Z_\beta = \sqrt{n} -Z_{\alpha/2}\) and \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma =1\) represent the parameters given for the Standard Normal Distribution from which \(Z_\beta = \sqrt{n} -Z_{\alpha/2}\) is calculated.

Part b

Now we can test the function to calculate the power when \(n = 10\), and \(\alpha = 0.05\):

# Test function
n <- 10
alpha <- 0.05
pnorm(q = sqrt(n)-qnorm(1-alpha/2, 0 , 1), mean = 0,sd = 1)
## [1] 0.885379

Part c

From here we can make a generalized version of this function that will accept \(n\), \(\delta\), \(\sigma\) and \(\alpha\) values:

# Define function
mypower <- function(n, delta, sigma, alpha){
  
  # Get Zbeta
  Zbeta <- (delta*sqrt(n)/sigma)-qnorm(1-alpha/2, 0 , 1)
  pwr <- pnorm(q = Zbeta, mean = 0,sd = 1)
  
  # Get beta
  beta <- 1-pwr
  
  # Plot
  nseq <- seq(0.001, n+20, length = 1000)
  Zbetas <- (delta*sqrt(nseq)/sigma)-qnorm(1-alpha/2, 0 , 1)
  pwrs <- pnorm(q = Zbetas, mean = 0,sd = 1)
  plot(nseq, pwrs, type = "l", 
       main =  bquote(bold(paste("Power Calculation: ",
                                 delta, " = ", .(delta), ", ",
                                 sigma, " = ", .(sigma), ", ",
                                 alpha, " = ", .(alpha)))),
       xlab = "n",
       ylab = "Power")
  
  # Outputs
  out <- list(power = pwr,
              beta = beta,
              n = n,
              delta = delta,
              alpha = alpha)
  
  return(invisible(out))
  
}

More Power

A python script was made and added to final package. The following code was used to make the python script:

import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import root_scalar
from scipy.stats import t as t_dist, nct

def power_t_test(n=None, delta=None, sd=1.0, power=None, sig_level=0.05, 
                 alternative="two.sided", type="two.sample", strict=False, tol=1e-8):
    
    # Validate that exactly one core parameter is None
    params = [n, delta, sd, power, sig_level]
    if sum(p is None for p in params) != 1:
        raise ValueError("exactly one of 'n', 'delta', 'sd', 'power', and 'sig_level' must be NULL")
    
    # Validation helpers for probabilities
    def assert_null_or_prob(val):
        if val is not None and not (0 <= val <= 1):
            raise ValueError("must be a probability between 0 and 1")
            
    assert_null_or_prob(sig_level)
    assert_null_or_prob(power)
    
    # Match arguments
    valid_types = ["one.sample", "two.sample", "paired"]
    if type not in valid_types:
        raise ValueError(f"'type' should be one of {', '.join(valid_types)}")
        
    valid_alts = ["two.sided", "one.sided"]
    if alternative not in valid_alts:
        raise ValueError(f"'alternative' should be one of {', '.join(valid_alts)}")
        
    tsample = 1 if type in ["one.sample", "paired"] else 2
    tside = 2 if alternative == "two.sided" else 1
    
    if tside == 2 and delta is not None:
        delta = abs(delta)
        
    # Define the power calculation function block using scipy.stats.nct
    def compute_power(n_val, delta_val, sd_val, sig_level_val):
        nu = max(1e-07, n_val - 1) * tsample
        # Critical value from standard central t-distribution
        qu = t_dist.ppf(1.0 - sig_level_val / tside, nu)
        
        # Non-centrality parameter
        ncp_val = np.sqrt(n_val / tsample) * delta_val / sd_val
        
        if strict and tside == 2:
            p1 = 1.0 - nct.cdf(qu, df=nu, nc=ncp_val)
            p2 = nct.cdf(-qu, df=nu, nc=ncp_val)
            return p1 + p2
        else:
            return 1.0 - nct.cdf(qu, df=nu, nc=ncp_val)

    # Solve for the missing parameter
    if power is None:
        power = compute_power(n, delta, sd, sig_level)
    elif n is None:
        res = root_scalar(lambda x: compute_power(x, delta, sd, sig_level) - power, 
                          bracket=[2.0, 1e7], xtol=tol)
        n = res.root
    elif sd is None:
        res = root_scalar(lambda x: compute_power(n, delta, x, sig_level) - power, 
                          bracket=[delta * 1e-07, delta * 1e7], xtol=tol)
        sd = res.root
    elif delta is None:
        res = root_scalar(lambda x: compute_power(n, x, sd, sig_level) - power, 
                          bracket=[sd * 1e-07, sd * 1e7], xtol=tol)
        delta = res.root
    elif sig_level is None:  
        res = root_scalar(lambda x: compute_power(n, delta, sd, x) - power, 
                          bracket=[1e-10, 1.0 - 1e-10], xtol=tol)
        sig_level = res.root
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("internal error")

    # Format output notes and methods
    note_map = {
        "paired": "n is number of *pairs*, sd is std.dev. of *differences* within pairs",
        "two.sample": "n is number in *each* group"
    }
    NOTE = note_map.get(type, None)
    
    type_label = {"one.sample": "One-sample", "two.sample": "Two-sample", "paired": "Paired"}[type]
    METHOD = f"{type_label} t test power calculation"
    
    # Return dictionary 
    return {
        "n": float(n),
        "delta": float(delta),
        "sd": float(sd),
        "sig.level": float(sig_level), 
        "power": float(power),
        "alternative": alternative,
        "note": NOTE,
        "method": METHOD
    }

# Define server logic
server <- function(input, output) {
  
  # Reactive arguments - updating calculations only when button clicked
  args <- eventReactive(input$update,{
    req(input$n, input$delta, input$sigma, input$alpha)
    list(
      n = input$n,
      delta = input$delta,
      sigma = input$sigma,
      alpha = input$alpha
    )
    
  }, ignoreNULL = FALSE)
  
  # Get results
  res <- reactive({
    
    args <- args()
    
    # Get Zbeta
    Zbeta <- (args$delta*sqrt(args$n)/args$sigma)-qnorm(1-args$alpha/2, 0 , 1)
    pwr <- pnorm(q = Zbeta, mean = 0,sd = 1)
    
    # Get beta
    beta <- 1-pwr
    
    # Plot
    nseq <- seq(0.001, args$n+20, length = 1000)
    Zbetas <- (args$delta*sqrt(nseq)/args$sigma)-qnorm(1-args$alpha/2, 0 , 1)
    pwrs <- pnorm(q = Zbetas, mean = 0,sd = 1)
    
    # Outputs
    out <- list(power = pwr,
                beta = beta,
                n = args$n,
                delta = args$delta,
                alpha = args$alpha,
                sigma = args$sigma,
                nseq = nseq,
                Zbetas = Zbetas,
                pwrs = pwrs)
    
    return(invisible(out))
    
  })
  
  # Click logic
  clck <- reactiveVal(NULL)
  
  # Get n and pwr values
  observeEvent(input$plot_click, {
    req(input$plot_click)
    
    
    current_args <- args()
    
    
    x <- input$plot_click$x
    
    
    Zbeta <- (current_args$delta * sqrt(x) / current_args$sigma) - qnorm(1 - current_args$alpha / 2, 0, 1)
    pwr <- pnorm(q = Zbeta, mean = 0, sd = 1)
    
    out <- list(pwr = pwr, x = x)
    
    clck(out)
  })
  
  # Click reset to remove crosshairs on plot
  observeEvent(input$dbl_click,{
    req(input$dbl_click)
    
    clck(NULL)
    
  })
  
  # Update to remove crosshairs on plot
  observeEvent(input$update,{
    req(input$update)
    
    clck(NULL)
    
  })
  
  # Plot for power calculations
  output$pwr <- renderPlot({
    
    res <- res()
    clck_val <- clck()
    
    # Main plot
    plot(res$nseq, res$pwrs, type = "l", 
         main =  bquote(bold(paste("Power Calculation: ",
                                   delta, " = ", .(res$delta), ", ",
                                   sigma, " = ", .(res$sigma), ", ",
                                   alpha, " = ", .(res$alpha)))),
         xlab = "n",
         ylab = "Power")
    
    # Crosshairs for click
    if (!is.null(clck_val)) {
      abline(v = clck_val$x, col = "blue", lty = 2)
      abline(h = clck_val$pwr, col = "blue", lty = 2)
      points(clck_val$x, clck_val$pwr, col = "blue", pch = 19, cex = 1.2)
    }
    
  })
  
  
  
  # Output for estimate calculations
  output$listout <- renderTable({
    res <- res()
    
    data.frame(
      "Power" = res$power,
      "Beta" = res$beta,
      "n" = res$n,
      "Delta" = res$delta,
      "Alpha" = res$alpha,
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }, align = "c", bordered = TRUE)
  
  # Output for click
  output$clickout <- renderTable({
    res <- clck()
    
    pwr <- if (is.list(res)) res$pwr else NA
    
    data.frame(
      "Power Calculation Along Curve From Click" = pwr,
      check.names = FALSE
    )
  }, align = "c", bordered = TRUE, digits = 4)
  
  # Output for the help card so user knows click options etc.
  output$help <- renderUI({
    HTML("Clicking anywhere on the plot will lock onto the plot curve and give you the calculated power at that point. Double click the plot to reset and remove the crosshairs.")
  })
}

# Run app
shinyApp(ui = ui, server = server)
